content.title: Identifying Relationships Between Variables
content.overview: In the ACT Science section, you must quickly determine how two variables relate to one another. This involves identifying whether a change in one variable (the independent variable) results in a consistent increase, decrease, or no change in another variable (the dependent variable).
learning_objectives: Define positive, negative, and no apparent relationships in data sets.
Apply the 3-Point Slope Check to classify data trends.
Distinguish between consistent trends and outliers or minor fluctuations.

sections.title: Types of Relationships
sections.content: A relationship describes how the dependent variable (usually 'y') behaves as the independent variable (usually 'x') increases. A Positive Relationship occurs when both variables move in the same direction; as x increases, y increases. A Negative Relationship occurs when variables move in opposite directions; as x increases, y decreases. No Apparent Relationship occurs when changes in x do not result in a predictable or consistent change in y, often appearing flat or scattered.

sections.title: The 3-Point Slope Check Strategy
sections.content:
To classify a relationship quickly and accurately, use the 3-Point Slope Check: 1. Compare the first and last data pairs to determine the overall direction. 2. Check one or two middle pairs to ensure the direction is consistent and not caused by a single outlier. 3. Estimate differences between neighboring pairs to see if the trend is steady, reversing, or flat. If the first-to-last direction matches at least half of the middle-pair differences, you can confidently label the relationship.

![A flowchart showing the three steps to identify a data relationship: Compare First/Last, Check Middle Pairs, and Estimate Differences.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/4f42f036-71ea-4604-a967-029e83d0cde2-1786506555302-408.webp)

sections.title: Consistency and Outliers
sections.content: Data in ACT Science passages may not be perfectly linear. A single data point that breaks the trend (an outlier) does not necessarily negate the overall relationship. If the majority of adjacent differences follow a specific direction, the relationship is still classified by that dominant trend. However, if the data reverses direction frequently or shows no net change from start to finish, it is classified as having no apparent relationship.

worked_examples.question:
A study measures the Solubility of a salt (g/100g water) at various Temperatures (°C):
Temp: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
Solubility: 35, 33, 28, 22, 15
Identify the relationship between Temperature and Solubility.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Compare first and last pairs. At 10°C, solubility is 35; at 50°C, it is 15. The value decreased, suggesting a negative relationship. Step 2: Check middle pairs. At 20°C (33) and 30°C (28), the values continue to drop. Step 3: Estimate adjacent differences (-2, -5, -6, -7). All differences are negative. Conclusion: There is a consistent negative relationship.

common_mistakes: Mistaking a single small increase or decrease at the end of a data set for a total change in relationship (e.g., 'leveling off').
Assuming a relationship exists when the first and last values are nearly identical.
Confusing the direction: remember that 'negative' means variables move in opposite directions, not that the values themselves are negative numbers.
exam_tips: Always look at the table or graph from left to right (increasing x-axis) to determine the trend.
If a question asks for a 'consistent' relationship, ensure there are no major reversals in the data points.
Ignore minor fluctuations if the overall start-to-finish trend is clear and supported by the majority of data points.
content.recap: To identify a relationship, compare the start and end points of the data, verify the trend with middle points, and ensure the majority of step-by-step changes follow the same direction. Positive trends go up, negative trends go down, and inconsistent trends show no apparent relationship.

knowledge_claims.content: A positive relationship exists when the dependent variable increases as the independent variable increases.
A negative relationship exists when the dependent variable decreases as the independent variable increases.
No apparent relationship exists when the dependent variable shows no consistent upward or downward trend as the independent variable changes.
The first step of the 3-Point Slope Check is to compare the first and last data pairs to determine the overall direction of change.
The second step of the 3-Point Slope Check involves checking middle data pairs to ensure the trend is consistent and not an outlier.
A relationship is considered consistent if the first-to-last direction matches at least half of the adjacent differences between data points.
In a negative relationship, the two variables move in opposite directions.
It is a mistake to classify a relationship as 'leveling off' based on a single smaller increment if the overall trend remains consistently upward or downward.
A flat line on a graph or identical values at the start and end of a table indicates no apparent relationship.
When analyzing a table, always observe how the dependent variable changes as the independent variable values increase numerically.
A positive relationship differs from a negative relationship in that the variables in a positive relationship move in the same direction.
An outlier is a data point that deviates from the overall trend but does not necessarily change the classification of the relationship if the majority of data is consistent.

SCIENCE PASSAGE 2: Dissolving Effervescent Tablets
Students tested how water temperature affects the time required for identical effervescent tablets to stop producing visible bubbles. In Experiment 1, they used 200 mL of water at four temperatures and one whole tablet per trial. In Experiment 2, they repeated the test with crushed tablets while keeping the water volume and temperatures unchanged.

According to the figure, what value was recorded for Whole tablet at the x-axis value 20?
F) 116
G) 152
H) 61
J) 68
items.explanation: Read the requested condition and series directly from the figure.

videoLesson.title: Determine Positive, Negative, or No Relationship
videoLesson.description: Recognize whether paired data trends upward, downward, or stays flat. Compare first and last pairs, then check middle pairs and estimate differences to confirm direction.
